items.title: Safety of direct cessation in infants under 8 weeks is unresolved
items.whyItMatters: The two relevant sources disagree and one is confounded, the other undated and unreviewed (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Keep stepwise weaning for infants under 8 weeks and collect their outcomes descriptively.

items.title: Night delivery of two-hourly checks
items.whyItMatters: Night checks are done by nurses alone and are often missed elsewhere (claim c4).
items.opportunity: Track trial-off timing and missed checks at night as process measures and adapt between cycles.

items.title: Last winter is a weak comparison
items.whyItMatters: Season severity, viral mix and staffing change from year to year, so a simple before-after comparison could mislead.
items.opportunity: Use weekly run charts with last winter as baseline points and annotate season changes.

items.title: Families not told the weaning criteria
items.whyItMatters: Parents with limited English or low health literacy are least likely to get consistent explanations.
items.opportunity: Give a plain-language criteria card, translated, at the start of high flow.

items.title: Readmissions to other hospitals are invisible
items.whyItMatters: Families living far away may return to a local hospital.
items.opportunity: Ask families at a 7-day phone call whether the infant was seen elsewhere.

errorsFound: The papers circulated by the PICU team were read as showing harm in all young infants; one is confounded by ward practice and the other finds no difference.
reevaluation: The gaps favour testing the protocol in improvement cycles for infants aged 8 weeks or older, with safety balancing measures, night process measures and stepwise weaning kept for younger infants.
summary: Five gaps: the young-infant conflict, night delivery, a weak historical comparison, family communication and invisible readmissions.
